notes.body:
The argument does not simply prove that someone, somewhere, once received knowledge from Allah rather than from a human teacher. It proves something more demanding: that this divine connection must be **present in every age**, because the need for instruction does not end. Each era is born just as ignorant as the last.

A lamp lit once and then left unattended will go out. The **prophet** is the lighting of the lamp — the original act of divine inspiration by which knowledge enters human history. The imam is the one who keeps it burning, age after age. Without someone in each era holding an unbroken connection to that source, every new generation would have a proof against Allah, saying: we found no one to guide us from falsehood to the truth.

There is also a difference in function. The prophet brings the revelation in its outer form — the law, the command, the prohibition. The imam holds its **inner meaning**, knowing how to draw from that revelation a living answer for every situation that arises after the prophet's era has closed.

The verse the passage cites makes this precise:

فَلِلَّهِ ٱلْحُجَّةُ ٱلْبَلِغَةُ

To Allah belongs the most apparent proof.
Al-An'am 6:149

A proof that existed once and is now absent is not a proof over those who came after. The imam, unique in his age, is how Allah's proof remains present and active — a **living, guiding reality**.

notes.quote: this in turn makes necessary a final end-point in the chain of teachers, namely the prophet and the imam
etymology: نبي (prophet): from the root ن-ب-أ, meaning to bring weighty news or a report from afar. The root marks the prophet as a carrier — someone who receives a transmission from beyond the human sphere and deposits it into the world. The word suggests arrival: something urgent has come, and he is its bearer.

إمام (imam): from the root أ-م-م, meaning to go before or stand in front. أمام means "in front of," making the imam literally the one others line up behind. The root is not about domination — it is about orientation: the imam is the direction everyone faces when they need to know which way to turn.

وحي (divine inspiration): from the root و-ح-ي, carrying the sense of swift, concealed communication — a whisper, a sign passed without words. The root captures that divine inspiration bypasses ordinary instruction entirely: direct, immediate, available only to its recipient. This is precisely what sets the prophet apart from every other link in the chain.

حجة (proof): from the root ح-ج-ج, which also gives حج, the pilgrimage. A حجة is not a sterile logical point — it is a proof that leads you somewhere, that draws you toward a destination. The imam as حجة is not merely evidence; he is a living path toward the truth.

notes.body:
The circle and the dot are not two separate qualities sitting side by side — they are two lenses focused on the same reality, from different distances. The circle tells us about the imam's **encompassing authority** within creation: every rank of the hierarchy (حدود) falls within his command, draws from him, and cannot stand without him, while he stands complete on his own. The dot tells us something deeper — not what the imam does, but what he essentially *is*: without parts, without a prior cause, the origin from which the line, the surface, and the body all unfold.

If we ask what is the imam's place in the world, the circle answers. If we ask whether we can fully know or describe the imam, the dot answers: it has no edges to trace, no sides to count, no interior to measure.

This is why the dot echoes what Maulana Ali taught: "the perfection of sincerity toward Him is the denial of attributes to Him, because every attribute bears witness that it is other than the thing described." The dot, having no parts, **admits no attribute** — you cannot say it is tall, wide, or coloured. In the same way, no one can rightly describe the imam's true nature; people can only confess their own inability to do so.

If either symbol takes precedence, it is the dot — as geometry itself demands. The line is a dot in motion; the circle is that line curved back upon itself. So the dot precedes the circle not only in rank but in generation: the imam's **unknowable essence** is the silent origin from which his encompassing authority flows.
notes.anchor: the dot, which the mathematicians describe as having no parts and as…
notes.quote: the dot, which the mathematicians describe as having no parts and as the origin of the line, the surface, and the body, is a symbol of the imam
etymology: نقطة (dot): from the root ن-ق-ط, meaning to drip or fall drop by drop. A single drop is indivisible and springs from nowhere else — it is the smallest unit. The geometric point carries the same quality: no interior, no parts, just the irreducible origin from which all extension begins.

دائرة (circle): from the root د-و-ر, meaning to turn or revolve. The word carries rotation within it — a دائرة is a turning that returns to itself. This motion of self-return is part of why the circle needs no other figure: it already contains its own completion.

حدود (ranks, limits): from the root ح-د-د, meaning to set a boundary or define. The singular حد means both a limit and a definition — to define something is to mark where it ends. The ranks of the hierarchy are called 'limits' because each one marks the reach of a degree of knowledge and authority.
